subject: mathematics_1b
question_text: Find the slope of the normal to the curve x = a cos³θ, y = a sin³θ at θ = π/4.

mark_split.label: Differentiate x and y with respect to θ
Slope of the normal at θ = π/4

recall_prompt: Say how you would do this one — say how you get dy/dx from a curve given through θ, what it simplifies to, and what you do to it at θ = π/4.

steps.label: Differentiate x and y with respect to θ
steps.margin_note: First mark. Both are cubes of a trigonometric function, so the chain rule applies twice over: cube first, then the inner function. The −sin θ inside dx/dθ is what makes the final slope negative.
lines: Given:   x = a cos³θ,   y = a sin³θ
Differentiate each with respect to θ, using the chain rule:
dx/dθ = a · 3cos²θ · (−sin θ) = −3a cos²θ sin θ
dy/dθ = a · 3sin²θ · (cos θ) = 3a sin²θ cos θ

recall.must_convey: That dx/dθ = −3a cos²θ sin θ and dy/dθ = 3a sin²θ cos θ.
accept: differentiate the cube first then the inside function
cos cubed gives three cos squared times minus sin
sin cubed gives three sin squared times cos
chain rule rendu sarlu apply cheyyali
dx by d theta is minus three a cos squared sin
the minus comes from differentiating cos theta

steps.why: cos³θ means (cos θ)³, so the power rule gives 3cos²θ and the chain rule then multiplies by the derivative of cos θ, which is −sin θ. The same pattern with sin θ carries no minus sign.
common_mistakes: Differentiating cos³θ to 3cos²θ and leaving out the −sin θ.
Writing dy/dθ with a minus sign, copying the minus from the x-derivative.
Reading cos³θ as cos(3θ) and differentiating to −3 sin(3θ).
steps.memory_tip: Differentiate the cube, then the inside. Only the cosine brings a minus sign out with it.

steps.label: Slope of the tangent
steps.margin_note: Second mark. 3a cancels, one sin θ and one cos θ cancel, and the minus sign stays. The result −tan θ holds at every point of the curve, so it is worth writing before substituting.
lines: For a curve given through θ:   dy/dx = (dy/dθ) / (dx/dθ)
dy/dx = 3a sin²θ cos θ / (−3a cos²θ sin θ)
Cancel 3a, one sin θ and one cos θ:

accept: divide dy by d theta by dx by d theta
three a cancels and one sin and one cos cancel
the slope of the tangent is minus tan theta
three a cancel ayi minus tan theta vasthundi
sin by cos is tan so the answer is minus tan theta
the tangent slope is minus tan theta at every point

steps.why: Dividing the two θ-derivatives cancels dθ and leaves the slope in θ alone. Cancelling one power from each of sin²θ and cos²θ leaves a single sin over a single cos, which is the tangent.
common_mistakes: Losing the minus sign and writing dy/dx = tan θ.
Cancelling both powers and writing dy/dx = −1.
Writing dy/dx = −cot θ, cancelling the wrong function from each.
steps.memory_tip: sin²/cos² divided the right way leaves sin/cos, which is tan. The minus comes from dx/dθ and stays.

steps.label: Slope of the normal at θ = π/4
steps.margin_note: The last two marks: one for the tangent slope at θ = π/4, one for turning it into the normal's. The question asks only for a SLOPE, so no line equation is needed.
lines: The normal is perpendicular to the tangent, so its slope is −1/m.

recall.must_convey: That m = −1 at θ = π/4 and the normal's slope is −1/m = 1.
accept: tan of pi by four is one so the tangent slope is minus one
the normal slope is minus one over minus one
the slope of the normal is one
tan forty five degrees one kabatti tangent slope minus one
minus one by minus one gives plus one
only the slope is asked so stop here
heard_as: slope of the normal is one

steps.why: tan(π/4) = 1, so the tangent has slope −1 and falls at 45°. The negative reciprocal of −1 is +1, so the normal rises at 45° — the two lines are perpendicular, and their slopes multiply to −1.
common_mistakes: Giving −1, which is the tangent's slope and not the normal's.
Working in degrees and using tan(π/4) as tan of about 0.785 degrees.
Writing a full line equation when only the slope is asked for.
steps.memory_tip: π/4 is 45°, where tan is 1. A slope of −1 and a slope of +1 are always perpendicular.
